lesson.title: The Other Doorway: How Allosteric Sites Control Enzymes from a Distance
lesson.summary: Allosteric regulation lets an activator or inhibitor bind a site away from the active site and reshape the whole enzyme, switching its activity on or off without ever touching the substrate binding pocket.
lesson.body:
The induced fit model already showed that enzymes are not rigid locks waiting for a key. Binding a substrate causes the active site to mold itself slightly around that substrate, a small conformational adjustment. Allosteric regulation takes that flexibility and turns it into a control system. Many enzymes have a second binding site, distinct from the active site and often located far away from it on the protein's surface, called an allosteric site. A regulatory molecule that binds there does not touch the active site directly, yet it can still switch the enzyme on or off.

The mechanism works through the enzyme's overall three dimensional shape. Because a protein's regions are physically connected and folded together, a small structural shift at the allosteric site propagates through the protein and reshapes the active site elsewhere in the molecule. If that reshaping makes the active site fit the substrate better, the bound molecule is called an activator. If it distorts the active site so substrate binds poorly or not at all, the bound molecule is an inhibitor. Either way, the regulation happens without the effector molecule ever entering the active site itself, which is what separates allosteric regulation from the direct active site competition seen in competitive inhibition.

Aspartate transcarbamoylase, the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis in bacteria, is a classic example. It is built from multiple subunits arranged so that ATP binding at an allosteric site signals that energy and building blocks are plentiful and activates the enzyme, while CTP, an end product of the very pathway the enzyme starts, binds a different allosteric site and inhibits it. The same protein integrates two opposite signals from two different allosteric sites, tuning its activity to the cell's actual needs rather than running at a fixed rate.

Many allosteric enzymes are also cooperative, meaning they are built from multiple subunits whose active sites influence one another. When substrate binds one subunit, it can nudge neighboring subunits into a conformation that binds substrate more readily, so the enzyme's activity accelerates sharply once it gets started. Plotting reaction rate against substrate concentration for a cooperative allosteric enzyme produces a sigmoidal, S shaped curve rather than the smooth hyperbola typical of simple, single site enzymes, a visible signature of subunits communicating with one another.

Because allosteric binding is reversible and noncovalent, cells can adjust enzyme activity within seconds in response to changing internal conditions, without having to make or destroy any protein. That speed and reversibility make allosteric regulation especially well suited to moment to moment metabolic control, including the feedback loops covered next, where a pathway's own end product reaches back to switch off the enzyme that started it.
